This served to significantly dilute the impact of OBC reservations. Currently, the court is also hearing a plea to apply the filter to Dalit and Adivasi quotas.

The fact that the Reservation Hatao Andolan is adopting this as a demand, even though it does not affect general category numbers, is thus not a paradox at all. It understands well how powerful a weapon creamy layer exclusion could be to weaken the small but vocal non-upper caste elites that reservations have created thus far.

editorials.title: 9/11 at 25: The day history changed direction
editorials.passage:
Some events do more than make history. They change its direction. The attacks of September 11, 2001, belong unmistakably to that category.

In less than two hours on that day, 19 terrorists struck at the symbols of American economic and military power, killed nearly 3,000 people and transformed the strategic priorities of the world’s most powerful nation. The images of aircraft disappearing into the Twin Towers and their subsequent collapse remain among the most defining visual memories of the modern age. Yet, 25 years later, the real significance of 9/11 lies less in the spectacle of that morning than in everything that followed.

The attacks interrupted an extraordinary period of post-Cold War optimism. The Berlin Wall had fallen in 1989, the Soviet Union had disappeared in 1991 and globalisation was gathering pace. US power appeared unchallengeable. Economic integration, technology and expanding international commerce seemed likely to define the emerging century.
9/11 abruptly changed the agenda. Terrorism, radicalisation, homeland security and military intervention replaced much of that optimism. History had taken a detour.
The Making of a Global Threat
The origins of 9/11 lay partly in an earlier conflict. The anti-Soviet jihad in Afghanistan during the 1980s brought together fighters, funding, ideology and networks from across the Islamic world. The Soviet withdrawal ended that war but not the ecosystem it had created.

Al-Qaeda emerged from this environment in 1988 and progressively transformed itself during the 1990s into a transnational terrorist organisation. Osama bin Laden sought to portray his confrontation with the US as part of a larger struggle on behalf of Islam. Attacks against American embassies in East Africa in 1998 and the USS Cole in 2000 demonstrated growing ambition and capability. Yet even these gave little indication of what was to come.

The extraordinary message of 9/11, viewed purely from the perspective of terrorist strategy, was the ability of a relatively small non-state organisation to compel the world’s pre-eminent power to reorder its priorities.

It also created something even more damaging: the perception of a civilisational confrontation. Extremist organisations claimed to speak for Islam while suspicion of Muslim communities grew in many Western societies and has not entirely disappeared yet. Radicalisation and Islamophobia began reinforcing each other. One of terrorism’s objectives is to create precisely such fractures within societies.

That was the success of 9/11.
When Terrorism Became War
The US response was expected and inevitable. Afghanistan was attacked in October 2001 and the Taliban regime rapidly collapsed. What initially appeared a spectacular military success, however, gradually became something quite different.

Counter-terrorism expanded into counter-insurgency; counter-insurgency into state-building; and state-building into an open-ended commitment whose political objectives became progressively less clear.

The Global War on Terror ultimately consumed enormous resources. Estimates of the wider cost of America’s post-9/11 wars run into several trillion dollars. The opportunity cost was equally significant: resources, institutions and national attention remained focused on terrorism and West Asia for almost two decades when they should have been focused on contesting China’s build-up.

There was also a strategic paradox of history. The US overwhelmingly defeated virtually every conventional military force it confronted. Yet military superiority repeatedly proved insufficient to produce enduring political outcomes. Afghanistan eventually joined Vietnam as another reminder that battlefield dominance and strategic success are not synonymous.
The final American departure from Kabul in August 2021, with the Taliban returning to power, brought that contradiction into particularly sharp relief.
Iraq and the Unintended War
Perhaps the most consequential secondary effect of 9/11 came in Iraq.

Iraq had no responsibility for the attacks, yet it is difficult to imagine the US invasion of 2003 without the political and psychological environment created by 9/11. The dismantling of the Iraqi state and security structures contributed to insurgency, sectarian conflict and the emergence of Al-Qaeda in Iraq (AQI), led by Al-Zarqawi.

From this violent ecosystem eventually arose ISIS.

ISIS went further than Al-Qaeda. It captured territory (even raised taxes), declared a caliphate in 2014, exploited social media with remarkable sophistication and attracted almost 40,000 recruits from across the world. Radical Islamist terrorism had moved from remote training camps into the consciousness, and sometimes the streets, of European and other societies.
Thus, an intervention undertaken in the atmosphere created by 9/11 actually triggered another security challenge requiring several years to contain.
The Security State That 9/11 Created
The consequences extended far beyond battlefields.

Airport security, intelligence sharing, terrorist-financing controls, surveillance, biometrics, border management and protection of critical infrastructure all expanded dramatically. The US created the Department of Homeland Security. NATO invoked Article 5, its collective-defence provision, for the first time in its history.

Much of this architecture remains with us.

There is something extraordinary about that achievement too. A terrorist organisation comprising perhaps a few thousand committed adherents ultimately changed aspects of the everyday behaviour of billions. Twenty-five years later, international travel, intelligence cooperation and domestic security still carry the imprint of 9/11.
India and the Terrorism Paradigm
For India, the revelation was less dramatic. We had already confronted Pakistan-sponsored terrorism in J&K for over a decade. What changed after 9/11 was the international understanding of the threat.

Then came the attack on India’s Parliament on December 13, 2001. The possibility that terrorists could strike at the institutional heart of a democracy no longer appeared theoretical.

Yet 9/11 produced a paradox for India. It gave greater international legitimacy to India’s warnings about cross-border terrorism, but simultaneously made Pakistan strategically indispensable to Washington’s campaign in Afghanistan. Pakistan became a frontline partner in the War on Terror even as extremist networks continued to find sanctuary and support within its territory.

That contradiction persisted for much of the next two decades and has been reinvented again recently.

India consequently strengthened counter-terrorism structures, intelligence coordination and internal-security capabilities. Kashmir too experienced the effects of a changing global attitude towards terrorism. The world had become less willing to romanticise armed extremist movements merely because they adopted the vocabulary of political grievance.
The Opportunity Cost of 9/11
Perhaps the most important consequence becomes visible only with hindsight.

While America fought terrorism, the international system was changing. China joined the World Trade Organization in December 2001, barely three months after 9/11. Over the next two decades it accumulated extraordinary economic, technological and military power. Russia gradually recovered strategic confidence. Cyber warfare, space, artificial intelligence and economic security began transforming the nature of national power.

Yet an enormous proportion of American strategic bandwidth remained absorbed by Afghanistan, Iraq and counter-terrorism.

It would be simplistic to argue that 9/11 caused China’s rise or America’s relative strategic distraction. But the question deserves asking: did the attacks divert American attention precisely when the foundations of the next great-power competition were being laid?
I may tend to think so.

The true cost of the Global War on Terror may therefore never be measurable only in dollars or casualties. It must also be measured in strategic attention.
The World It Left Behind
The withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 closed one circle, but terrorism did not disappear. Al-Qaeda is diminished and ISIS lost its territorial caliphate, yet extremist networks survive in different forms across parts of Asia, West Asia and Africa. The threat has fragmented rather than vanished.

The international system, meanwhile, has moved elsewhere. China, Russia, Ukraine, the Indo-Pacific, technology, supply chains, cyber and space increasingly dominate strategic thinking.
That leaves perhaps the greatest irony of 9/11.

The terrorists did not defeat the US, nor did they create the world they sought. But they succeeded in diverting the strategic energy of the world’s most powerful nation for almost two decades.

And while the US fought them, history did not stand still.

(The author is Governor of Bihar, former Member of NDMA and former Commander of India’s Srinagar-based Chinar Corps. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Head-on | Resetting ties with Xi Jinping is India’s key Brics agenda
editorials.passage:
Chinese President Xi Jinping was last in India in 2019. Seven years later, much has changed. Contrary to popular belief, the change has been largely to China’s disadvantage.

In 2019, China’s GDP was $14.56 trillion. In 2026, its GDP is $20.86 trillion — a growth of 40 per cent in seven years. That’s a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6 per cent, the lowest since the Chinese economic miracle began 30 years ago.

It gets worse. China’s GDP growth rate in 2027 is estimated to fall below 4 per cent for the first time in 40 years and further to 3 per cent through the 2030s.

Chinese analysts shrug off these numbers. Artificial intelligence (AI), electric vehicles (EVs), automation, semiconductors and humanoid robots, they say, will turbocharge productivity, neutralising the effects of an ageing, shrinking population. But will they?

China’s economy, despite its dazzling technology and infrastructure, is hollowing out from the inside. With up to 70 per cent of the average Chinese household’s wealth locked in real estate, the plunge in property prices has led to a collapse in domestic consumption. Chinese warehouses are packed with unsold EVs and electronic goods. Most are being exported to Europe and Southeast Asia below cost prices, leading to a backlash from France and Germany.

Xi’s policies since he took charge as president in 2013 have contributed to China’s economic malaise. In 2013, it was widely accepted that China’s GDP would close the gap with US GDP within a decade and overtake it by the mid-2030s.

No one says that anymore, not even the Chinese. The gap between the US and Chinese economies has remained static at over $10 trillion. At its expected 2027 growth rate of 3 per cent, and falling, that gap will not close.

Xi has been anti-industry, reprising the role Mao Zedong played during the Cultural Revolution of 1966-76. Like Mao, Xi has prioritised social order over entrepreneurship. His treatment of Alibaba founder Jack Ma telegraphed the distaste he felt for business leaders.

Despite being awash with cash from China’s large trade surplus of $1.2 trillion, Xi delayed a stimulus to cash-starved local municipalities, citing their high debt levels. On Xi’s watch, China’s national, corporate and household debt has climbed to over $60 trillion. Its debt-to-GDP ratio has soared to 300 per cent.

Jason Ma wrote in Fortune magazine: “Beijing is aware of its debt situation, particularly among local governments that often seek to boost favored industries like AI, electric vehicles, and robotics with low-cost loans. Chinese companies are borrowing more than they are selling. Business debt has doubled since 2019, while revenues are only 30 per cent higher. Creditors continue to roll over loans to keep struggling firms afloat, even as nearly one-third of them are losing money.”

Will AI save China? Unlikely. AI and automation can boost productivity in a shrinking workforce, but they can’t defuse a demographic time bomb.

The mellower version of Xi at the Brics 2026 leaders’ summit on September 12-13 in New Delhi will be visibly different from the Xi seen at his last informal summit with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at Mahabalipuram in 2019.

In the pre-Covid era, China’s economy was racing ahead at over 8 per cent a year. Beijing had bullied the littoral nations of the Indo-Pacific into quiet subservience. The Mahabalipuram summit with Modi was Xi’s third and final effort to wean PM Modi out of the US orbit.

That effort had begun with a swing ride with PM Modi in Ahmedabad on the banks of the Sabarmati River in September 2014, followed by a second informal summit in Wuhan in 2018. A third summit in Mahabalipuram in October 2019 convinced Xi that PM Modi would not abandon — or even dilute — India’s long-term geopolitical relationship with the US. Within months, Chinese troops engaged in a violent confrontation with Indian soldiers in eastern Ladakh’s Galwan Valley.

China simultaneously increased military and economic support to Pakistan. Investments between India and China went into deep freeze. The subsequent thaw in relations over the past year has many touchpoints. First, India’s near-8 per cent economic growth despite trade turmoil, $100 oil prices and the Gulf war has not gone unnoticed in Beijing.

India is now growing twice as fast as China. With its demographic dividend likely to peak in the mid-2030s and last till the early 2050s, India’s future economic growth will be driven by a young, productive, upskilled workforce, a growing middle class, and rising purchasing power.

Beijing’s relationship with Washington, meanwhile, has deteriorated from being trading partners to adversarial competitors. Xi has noted India’s cooler approach to a US trade deal. New Delhi has deliberately delayed signing a Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) that Modi and Trump had greenlit nearly 18 months ago at their White House meeting in February 2025.

A closer relationship with India at this stage suits Xi. He is approaching a controversial fourth successive term in 2027-28. No Chinese leader has served more than three consecutive terms as president since Mao. Internal pressure against Xi from the Communist Party of China (CPC) is building up.

The Taiwan question too hangs heavy over Xi’s head. He had let it be known that Taiwan would be united with China by 2027, by force if necessary. After seeing the difficulty two military superpowers, the US and Russia, are encountering in defeating much smaller enemies, Iran and Ukraine respectively, Xi will be rethinking his 2027 timeline for invading Taiwan.

None of these issues, however, will weigh directly on the Brics 2026 summit. With Russian President Vladimir Putin in New Delhi this week, the chemistry between Putin, Xi and Modi will not go unnoticed in Washington, nor will the presence of Iran and efforts to de-dollarise trade between the Brics member nations.

The combined nominal GDP of the 11-nation Brics group at $30.86 trillion is rapidly catching up with the G7’s combined nominal GDP of $48.94 trillion. Measured by purchasing power parity (PPP), Brics’ combined GDP of $91.3 trillion is already far ahead of the G7’s combined GDP (PPP) of $62.3 trillion.

That, too, will not go unnoticed in the Trump White House.

(The writer is an editor, author and publisher. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Brics 2026: India faces a tough consensus test
editorials.passage:
The 18th Brics Summit, hosted by India in New Delhi on September 12-13, is taking place in exceptional circumstances. The geopolitical backdrop is far more complex than it was a year ago. Brics has never had to reconcile so many competing geopolitical interests inside a single negotiating room.

When Brazil hosted the previous summit in July last year, the multilateral trading system already stood challenged by what the declaration termed the proliferation of trade-restrictive actions in the form of indiscriminate increases in tariffs and non-tariff measures. Since then, the issue of tariffs has worsened. The conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza were already enduring wars at the previous summit; since then, another protracted war has broken out in West Asia, with no end in sight.

Since its establishment, the Brics grouping has expanded to eleven full members. South Africa was admitted in 2010. Egypt, Ethiopia, Saudi Arabia, Iran and the UAE joined in 2024, followed by Indonesia in 2025. The presence of belligerents in the ongoing West Asia war — Iran on the one hand and Saudi Arabia and the UAE on the other — adds a new layer of complexity to the efforts to forge consensus on a joint declaration. It may be recalled that India succeeded in fostering consensus during its G20 presidency, notwithstanding differences among G20 members over the war in Ukraine.

From India’s point of view, the forthcoming summit provides a fresh opportunity to highlight issues of importance to the Global South, framed by its value-based, “people first” and human-centric approach. Over the past year, India has held 350 meetings and high-level engagements around the country. These have covered crucial issues such as agriculture and food security, holistic healthcare, skilling, energy security, urban infrastructure, industrial resilience for MSMEs, support for start-ups, global supply and value chains, as well as youth and sports.

The US and Western countries are apprehensive that Brics is taking on an anti-Western hue. From India’s perspective, however, it is better described as a non-Western grouping — perhaps a foil to the G7 — rather than an anti-Western one. Many Brics members today, including India, have close ties with the West.

The real issue concerning Brics is, therefore, not that it is confronting the West. It is about its ability to hold together a grouping whose members increasingly have conflicting interests.

President Donald Trump has said that “Brics is dead”. He has also alleged that Brics is attempting “de-dollarisation” to undermine the US currency and threatened sanctions on Brics member states. The Brics declarations, however, have never explicitly called for de-dollarisation, but the message is equally clear: members do not want to be held hostage by others. The emphasis last year was on the New Development Bank expanding finance in local currencies, the potential for greater interoperability of Brics payment systems, and safe cross-border payments among Brics countries. This sentiment may be expected to prevail this year in view of the growing interface between geopolitics and geo-economics.

Trump’s irritation may also stem from the fact that the Brics summit held in Rio de Janeiro on July 6-7, 2025, condemned the military strikes against the Islamic Republic of Iran as a violation of international law and the UN Charter. Both the Iran-Israel 12-Day War and the US’ Operation Midnight Hammer of last year stand dwarfed by the scale of conflict this year. Not only are Israel, the US and Iran involved, but the Gulf states are increasingly drawn into the fray.

The conflict has altered the positions of Brics members themselves, making last year’s formulations politically inadequate this year.

One can, therefore, expect that the Brics declaration this year will not find it easy simply to condemn the military strikes on Iran. With both Saudi Arabia and the UAE in the room, the language will have to be more balanced. Perhaps the negotiators will limit themselves to borrowing a line from the recent Bishkek SCO Declaration, which expressed “deep concern over developments in West Asia and around Iran” and “grave concern over the escalation of the situation in the Middle East”.

Unlike the SCO declarations, in which members, with the exception of India, express their support for China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), Brics declarations do not refer to China’s initiatives, whether the BRI or the Four Global Initiatives.

There is also the question of how the declaration will frame the issue of reform of the UN, including the Security Council. Brics traditionally refers to the Johannesburg-II Leaders’ Declaration, the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration, underscoring the need to make the UN and its organs more democratic, representative, effective and efficient, besides increasing the representation of developing countries in the UNSC. A similar thrust is expected to continue on the need to reform the Bretton Woods Institutions (BWI) to enhance the voice and representation of Emerging Markets and Developing Economies (EMDEs).

Last year, the Brics Summit condemned the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir on April 22, 2025, besides reaffirming the commitment of member states to combating the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens. From India’s point of view, it will be important to continue with language expressing strong condemnation of acts of terrorism. This should not be difficult. But the larger challenge is whether it can persuade an increasingly heterogeneous Brics to reconcile internal differences on the ongoing geopolitical churn.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s consistent call for an early end to the endless wars and advocacy of peace should help.

(The author is the Director General of the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Summit to farm: The real Brics test
editorials.passage:
With just a day to go before the Brics Summit, the question is no longer how much weight the expanded grouping carries, but what it can actually deliver. Agriculture could be its most practical test. Brics brings together some of the world’s largest producers, consumers and exporters of food, yet millions of its farmers remain vulnerable to climate shocks, volatile prices, rising input costs, trade barriers and fragile supply chains. If Brics wants to turn the promise of the Global South into tangible outcomes, it could begin with the farm.

Half the World, Shared Farm Challenges

Brics countries hold 42 per cent of the world’s farmland and nearly half its population. Of the roughly 510 million farms worldwide operating on less than two hectares, about 372 million, nearly 73 per cent, are in Brics countries. In India, China, Indonesia, Ethiopia and Egypt, such small holdings make up more than 85 per cent of all farms. Strengthening the smallholder farmer, therefore, means strengthening the food system itself.

These countries may have very different agricultural systems, but their farmers increasingly confront the same pressures. Weather is becoming less predictable. Seeds, fertilisers and other inputs are becoming more expensive. Prices remain uncertain, while access to markets, credit, insurance and technology remains uneven. Supply-chain disruptions add another layer of risk. For small and family farmers, even one failed crop or sudden price shock can wipe out a season’s income. These are no longer isolated farming problems. Together, they pose a larger challenge to food security, rural livelihoods and agricultural resilience across the members.

This combination of scale and vulnerability makes smallholders central to the Brics agricultural agenda. They are not merely food producers. They sustain food security, rural livelihoods and the resilience of agricultural systems.

Different Pathways, Common Purpose

Across Brics, countries have developed different ways to support small farmers. Brazil’s PRONAF, India’s Kisan Credit Card and PM-KISAN, South Africa’s CASP and Indonesia’s agricultural credit programmes offer different models for improving access to finance, insurance and markets.

Similar innovative approaches are emerging for women and youth, from India’s Krishi Sakhi and Namo Drone Didi and Ethiopia’s joint land certification to China’s New Professional Farmers and the UAE’s Youth Council for Agriculture. Together, these experiences make Brics a laboratory of practical solutions. The opportunity now is not to replicate one model everywhere, but to learn from what works, adapt it to local conditions and scale successful approaches, particularly those that empower women and make agriculture more attractive to the next generation.

By exchanging proven solutions, technologies and best practices, countries can strengthen the resilience of their agricultural systems, empower small farmers and build more secure and sustainable food systems.

The Indore Blueprint

Brics provides a unique platform to address shared agricultural challenges through cooperation and learning from each other’s experiences. As part of India’s Brics agriculture track, the Agriculture Ministers’ Meeting was held in Indore in June 2026, led by Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan. The meeting culminated in the Indore Declaration, laying out a roadmap for deeper agricultural cooperation among Brics countries.

Building on existing cooperation, the declaration places farmers more explicitly at the centre of the Brics agricultural agenda and recognises common vulnerabilities. It links food security to farmers’ livelihoods and productive capacity, particularly for small and family farmers, women and youth. It focuses on improving their access to technology, knowledge, markets and opportunities.

Importantly, it recognises that one-size-fits-all approaches may not reflect diverse national and local realities and can place disproportionate burdens on smallholders. It therefore calls for farmer-centric approaches that are tailored to national circumstances.

The Indore Declaration also launched several practical initiatives. Brics Agrin aims to promote cooperation on better seeds, fertilisers and bio-inputs. A new Farmers’ Rights Forum in seed systems aims to protect farmers’ interests and traditional knowledge. Brics also created networks for climate-friendly farming and digital agriculture, including AI, satellite information and digital farm advice. Further, strengthening the existing Brics Agricultural Research Platform as a Knowledge-to-Action Hub will help turn research into practical solutions that farmers can use.

These initiatives can help farmers access better seeds, save water, reduce input costs and use digital information on weather, crops and markets. The Brics ministers therefore agreed to strengthen applied, field-tested research and improve the dissemination of proven solutions. The message is clear: cooperation must move from knowledge to action, and from laboratory to land.

What Delhi Must Deliver

The Indore Declaration has provided the roadmap. The Brics Summit must now provide political momentum. The priority should be to identify proven solutions that can travel across Brics, from climate-resilient seeds and affordable farm technologies to digital advisory systems, credit and market-access models.

Smallholders, women and young farmers should remain at the heart of this effort. This would also give Brics a distinctly people-centric character, where cooperation is measured not only by declarations and institutions, but by improvements in people’s lives.

For a grouping that seeks to amplify the voice of the Global South, few places better demonstrate delivery than the farms that feed it. Brics has the scale, Indore has provided the roadmap, and the summit now has the opportunity to deliver for the farmer and the future.

(Prof. Sachin Kumar Sharma is Director General, and Lakshmi Swathi Ganti is a consultant at RIS, a Delhi-based think tank. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the authors. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Vikram's Murder Isn't Just 'Senseless' Violence. It’s a Symptom of a Lonely City
editorials.passage: Chongtham Vikram Singh, a 54-year-old guitarist and music teacher from Manipur, succumbed after an alleged assault below his Southeast Delhi home, reportedly for objecting to late-night shouting and disturbance.Official procedures began—the police registered a murder case and apprehended suspects. The investigation must now move with speed, clarity and an unblinking sense of consequence. It is ironic and reflects an X-ray of civic decay, that a musician who turned sound into music was beaten into silence for asking for silence. Noise parades as entitlement, and a plea for peace is heard as provocation. The assailants' anger wears a costume of power, and fearing the consequences of supporting the victim, people remain silent behind closed doors.Vikram stood tall, then fell to the assault—a musician from Manipur's pioneering Western-rock scene, and a teacher to younger musicians. His death echoes a darker rhythm—a country learning to hear outrage as noise, and human distress as somebody else's song.Manipuri Musician Killed in Delhi Was Threatened By Accused Before, FIR SaysIn Rashomon, Japanese director Akira Kurosawa's great film about truth, fear, and human frailty, several men seek refuge from rain beneath an old city gate. The gate still stands, but has long ceased to protect anyone. Broken, abandoned and scoured hollow by time, it gives them a roof but neither safety nor clarity.Delhi's neighbourhoods are India's Rashomon-ruined gates. They bristle with an armoury of protection—gates, guards, cameras, biometric entries, resident welfare associations (RWAs), surveillance screens, and patrols. Nevertheless, this elaborate grammar of safety is often only a false ceiling above fear. Beneath it, a resident can still stand unprotected at the doorstep.A home should be a haven, a place to sleep, rest or ask for quiet without fear. A neighbourhood should be its first ring of protection. Instead, gated compounds have become private islands facing a public wasteland—secure in appearance, solitary in fact.Indian citizens remember delivery apps and security agencies, but not always the name across the landing. An argument rises, a group gathers, menace roughens the air, and then the small, fatal arithmetic comes to mind: what will involvement in trying to stop it cost the victim? At that moment, the gate remains locked, the camera keeps recording, and shelter disappears.The fear is real—that menace can turn on anyone who intervenes, and thus civic life is reduced to reckless heroism or total withdrawal. Yes, between those extremes lies the necessary work of courage required by the neighbour—calling the police before violence crests, informing a residents' group, and refusing to disappear behind a locked door.Such acts may not prevent the worst. But they refuse abandonment. Delhi's gate collapses further whenever private security is mistaken for collective safety.After public violence, India and its neighbours ask, almost by reflex, "Was there CCTV?" The question is necessary. Footage can preserve evidence, trace movement, and strengthen an investigation. In Vikram's case, Delhi Police have said CCTV footage is under examination.But the camera is just an alibi for conscience, an unblinking eye that creates the illusion that someone was watching, but no one was.It archives the suffering but does not call for help, interrupt a blow, or become the neighbour. It is a cold instrument of the surveillance age, allowing citizens to mistake recording for responsibility and spectatorship for concern.Vikram's case requires prompt, rigorous, and conclusive investigation. However, certain truths must remain beyond negotiation. A citizen has the right to object to nuisance outside a home, and Vikram's request for quiet was not provocation. A disagreement is not a licence for a beating. Moral numbness has its own routine, it drafts explanations before it accepts responsibility.Between Murder and Mob Lynching: An MP Court's Unusual VerdictVikram's killing summons another image—the waiting citizens of India. In Waiting for Godot, the celebrated play by Nobel Prize-winning writer Samuel Beckett, two men stand beneath a bare tree in a barren landscape, waiting for a figure expected but never arriving; time passes, and words circle, but nothing changes. The waiting becomes the existence of life.Has the Indian citizen made a similar ritual of waiting? Not for one absent man, but for the first decisive act that might break the spell of numbness. After a killing, citizens wait for police action, a swift legal process, official responsibility, and television outrage. Nonetheless, the next tragedy often arrives before the last has found an ending, and the waiting goes on.The neighbours wait for the police, who wait for procedure and directions from higher authorities. Political leaders wait for public mood. Citizens wait for someone braver to begin the work of decency. The dead wait for justice that arrives too late to save them.This waiting is crowded with rituals, condolences, candlelight marches, studio debates, hashtags and public grief. But little shifts. The wheel turns, and the waiting goes on. Public feeling is brief, scattered and easily redirected to the next event. For grief has become consumable, and there is just numbness of existence.In a country accustomed to repeated violence, waiting is an arrangement that protects the violent.NHRC’s Blind Spot on Mob Lynchings—And HC Judge Who Finally Said it Out LoudTo call such killings "senseless" registers shock, but obscures the social logic from which violence grows. A society does not turn cruel by accident. Cruelty is built from small permissions such as an insult excused, a threat ignored, a crowd emboldened, a neighbour looking away. Each seems minor; together, they pave the road to brutality.Vikram's killing should unsettle every citizen because its pattern is becoming familiar. The same impulse surfaces in road rage, domestic violence, caste humiliation, communal threats, attacks on migrants, harassment of women, and political intimidation. Although issues and scenery shift, habits endure. Someone decides another person's dignity is expendable, while others learn to tolerate that decision.Vikram's death belongs to this wider landscape. Every act of violence does not need to have the same cause for it to reveal the same dangerous social habit—the growing permission to humiliate, threaten or harm another human being without expecting anyone to intervene. His death in Delhi is therefore not an exception, but a national symptom.The capital holds the country in miniature, where private security meets public fear; polished infrastructure beside exhausted citizenship; elite speech beside street-level impunity. Gates rise everywhere, yet shelter recedes. Fear moves freely through a country that fortifies its homes while leaving its people unprotected. That is how brutality becomes ordinary. Not because an entire society suddenly becomes violent, but because the boundaries of what it is prepared to tolerate keep moving.Vikram's Manipuri identity deepens the moral meaning of his death. Since ethnic violence erupted in Manipur in May 2023, lives have been lost, families displaced, homes burnt, and faith in public institutions steadily scorched away. However, the nation remains silent, and Manipur enters the national imagination as an intermittent flicker through an information blackout—one unbearable image, a brief outrage, a political exchange, then silence.For many people from Manipur and the wider Northeast, Delhi is a city of possibility, but a shadow remains—the experience of being treated as foreign in one's own country. And Vikram came from a region whose anguish has repeatedly been exiled from national feeling. He then died in the capital after allegedly objecting to noise outside his home.Highlighting the metaphor's severity, Manipur asks the country to hear its suffering; a musician asks men to lower their voices. Both appeals too often meet dismissal, indifference, or force.Vikram is not a convenient symbol to be briefly mourned and then forgotten. He was a musician, teacher, son and member of a community. His family deserves justice and accountability, just as Manipur, Manipuri and Northeast communities deserve more than ceremonial sympathy.‘Chinky’, ‘Chinese’: The Everyday Racism Faced by People from Northeast IndiaRegardless, the ruined gate need not be the final image. In Kurosawa's Rashomon, amid stories of deceit and cruelty, a fragile possibility survives— human beings remain capable of care. That slender thread is an answer to public cynicism, not because it promises rescue, but because it refuses to abandon another person to the rain.Vikram's killing exposes a wider numbness. The citizen must stop waiting. Responsibility begins before a crowd becomes a mob—a neighbour who notices, a witness who calls, a residents' group that acts, a refusal to treat drunkenness as an alibi. Vikram could have remained upstairs. Instead, he stood at the threshold of a larger question: what has happened to the Indian citizen's capacity to hear another human being?The country cannot wait beneath a barren tree for a rescuer who will never come. Nor can it shelter beneath a ruined gate while rain enters through every crack. Law, policing and institutions are indispensable, but shelter must also be rebuilt through the daily discipline of recognising another person's fear as a shared responsibility.Vikram asked for quiet, and the answer cannot be silence.(Navina Jafa is a cultural activist, classical Kathak dancer, and independent cultural historian who writes on the intersections of culture, politics, and social issues. She is also an expert in heritage tourism and cultural-skills mapping. This is an opinion piece and the views expressed are the author’s own. editorials.title: If BAPS Is India’s Soft Power, PM Modi Can’t Wash His Hands of Its Fallout
editorials.passage: In 2015, Prime Minister Narendra Modi played a pivotal and direct role in getting permission and the land grant to build the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) temple in Abu Dhabi. The breakthrough occurred during Modi’s official visit to the UAE in August 2015, the first by an Indian PM in 34 years. According to a top UAE diplomat, President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahayan took just “five minutes” to approve Modi’s request for a Hindu temple in the Gulf country where large number of Indian and Hindu expatriates reside. The temple was inaugurated by Modi in 2024.Since Modi came to power, BAPS has functioned as a premier vehicle for India’s cultural diplomacy. From the high-profile inauguration of the Abu Dhabi temple to major events in the US and Europe, the ruling dispensation has consistently integrated the organisation’s sprawling global network into its foreign policy apparatus.These grand temples serve dual purposes: they act as spiritual hubs for the diaspora and as diplomatic assets that project a civilisational identity on the global stage.Removal of Female Staff During Hindu Group's Visit at Eiffel Tower Sparks RowLast week’s episode at the Eiffel Tower, however, has brought out the perils of a modern, secular nation using a sect with a retrograde outlook on gender equality for public diplomacy. The actions of a group of saffron-clad monks of BAPS, led by their supreme spiritual leader Mahant Swami Maharaj, has made it appear as though the entire Hindu faith comprises of misogynists of an extreme variety.On 6 September, when Modi virtually addressed the inauguration of the grand BAPS temple in the Parisian suburb of Bussy-Saint-Georges, the event was framed as a historic milestone for India’s global soft power. The Indian flag formed a prominent backdrop, India’s ambassador to France was in attendance, and the message was clear: BAPS was a vital partner in New Delhi’s international diaspora strategy.In his remarks, Modi had referred to the India-France Strategic partnership and praised the construction of the temple providing “a completely new dimension to the possibilities of joint ventures.”On Saturday, 5 September, a day before the inauguration of the temple, a delegation of some 100 members from the BAPS sect visited the Eiffel Tower. The visiting delegation reportedly wanted no interaction with women and asked that female employees stay out of sight. The management of the Eiffel Tower complied and asked female staff to leave their posts and avoid certain areas. They were replaced by male colleagues.Workers and union representatives of the Eiffel Tower complex staged a walkout on Monday, 7 September, calling the directive humiliating and a violation of professional equality. The historic landmark remained shut that day.The across-the-board outrage in France and elsewhere compelled the Paris municipality and the Eiffel Tower authorities to apologise, agreeing that BAPS should never have been accommodated. BAPS also apologised, claiming that they did not practice intentional gender bias.As soon as the group’s celibacy protocols triggered a political storm at the Eiffel Tower, the Indian government immediately dumped the hot potato and claimed that the whole thing had nothing to do with the government—and the dispute was “purely between the entities concerned.”  The Swaminarayan sect is mainly Gujarati in its core membership and cultural practices, but curiously enough, its founder and the person its members consider the supreme deity, Lord Swaminarayan, was born as Ghanshyam Pande, near Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh. He travelled across India and settled down in Gujarat in the early 19th century.BAPS swamis are of course not the only religious people who advocate celibacy and a separation of sexes. It is well-known that Roman Catholic and Buddhist monks, too, follow such practices. The swamis and monks are free to maintain their practices in their own spaces, but the problem occurs when such practices are foisted on unsuspecting people, as was done at the Eiffel Tower.In Mohan Bhagwat's NYC Visit, a Divided Diaspora & 'New Definition' of a HinduA friend of a friend recounted a two-decade-old story of a commercial flight to Kenya with the BAPS monks taking over the aircraft, which had only male stewards who served vegetarian meals and no alcohol. She and other “normal” (and female) passengers were segregated at the back and kept in check by two bouncers.BAPS power in India has grown exponentially with the political power of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which, of course, has been dominant in Gujarat for a while. During the Atal Bihari Vajpayee years, they decided to make a grand temple in New Delhi. It was built at a prominent place opposite India Gate, on what most environmentalists say is the ecological floodplain of the Yamuna River, while the authorities claim it has been built on the river bank. Thereafter, the Supreme Court and the National Green Tribunal have given it a clean chit.The problem, as the Paris episode revealed, is that the organisation’s core beliefs can be antithetical not only to modern global norms, but also to the principles on which secular and equal India was founded. In India, secularism means equality among religions, though it is unlikely that the PM would be involved in inaugurating a mosque or a gurdwara abroad. French laïcité (strict secularism), and its commitment to gender equality, is more unforgiving and deeply institutionalised.If New Delhi wants to exploit the global prestige generated by its diaspora’s religious institutions, it must also be prepared to inherit the political liabilities that come with it when those institutions clash with the foundational values of their host nations.(The writer is a Distinguished Fellow, Observer Research Foundation, New Delhi. This is an opinion piece, and the views expressed above are the author’s own. The Quint neither endorses nor is responsible for the same.)
